title: Constant-factor truthful-in-expectation scheduling
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(K\ge1\) such that, for every machine count \(m\ge2\), some family of truthful-in-expectation mechanisms handles every finite job count \(n\ge1\) and every finite nonnegative real processing-time matrix \(t\) with \[\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]\le K\operatorname{OPT}(t)?\] Here \(C(\sigma,t)\) is the makespan of assignment \(\sigma\), as defined below. The factor is independent of \(m,n,t\); arbitrary correlated random assignments and payments are allowed, and computation is unrestricted.
definitions:
\[R(m)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_m}\ \sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0}}
\frac{\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(t)}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_m\) consists of the families satisfying the incentive and zero-optimum conditions below. 

Jobs, machines and private costs. Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). There are \(m\ge2\) machines and \(n\ge1\) indivisible jobs. Machine \(i\) has a private type \(t_i=(t_{i1},\ldots,t_{in})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Executing a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). All entries are finite; zero is allowed. The times on different machines and jobs have no promised relation. Every job is assigned exactly once, and all jobs assigned to one machine are executed sequentially. There are no release times, precedences, eligibility restrictions, migration, preemption or interactions between different jobs' costs.

Direct mechanisms. Reports have the same domain as types. For each report matrix \(b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\), a mechanism specifies numbers
\[q_\sigma(b)\ge0\quad(\sigma:[n]\to[m]),\qquad\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(b)=1,\]
and a finite real expected payment \(p_i(b)\in\mathbb R\) to each machine. Thus the outcome at each fixed report is a distribution on the finite set of \(m^n\) assignments. Define the marginal assignment probability
\[x_{ij}(b)=\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(j)=i}q_\sigma(b).\]
The numbers \(q_\sigma(b)\) may be arbitrary reals, and assignments of different jobs need not be independent. Payments can be deterministic amounts \(p_i(b)\): allowing random payments with finite expectations makes no difference to the risk-neutral utility or objective here. Positive payments are received by the machine. No individual rationality, budget balance, sign restriction, transfer bound, anonymity or task-independence condition is imposed.

Truthfulness in expectation. For every machine \(i\), true type \(t_i\), alternative report \(b_i\), and fixed reports \(b_{-i}\) of all other machines, require
\[p_i(t_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{-i})
\ \ge\ p_i(b_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{-i}).\]
This is the dominant-strategy condition for expected payment minus true processing cost. Only one agent's report changes in this comparison. There is no prior distribution on types, expectation over other players' reports, or assumption that those reports are honest. The expectation is over the mechanism's own allocation randomness. Truthfulness of each deterministic rule obtained by fixing a random seed is not required.

Performance. When the report matrix equals the true matrix \(t\), an assignment has makespan
\[C(\sigma,t)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}t_{ij},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min_{\sigma:[n]\to[m]}C(\sigma,t).\]
The expectation in the formal statement is the finite sum \(\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(t)C(\sigma,t)\). It is the expected maximum load, not the maximum of the expected loads. Payments do not enter the makespan. The optimum uses the same machines and jobs with full knowledge of the true processing times. For every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\), an admissible mechanism must have expected makespan zero; division by zero is omitted from the displayed supremum. All positive-optimum instances and all job counts are included, with no additive error term.

Optimization over mechanisms. For a fixed \(m\), a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_m\) precisely when each member has the stated domain and satisfies truthfulness and the zero-optimum condition at every report profile. Its supremum ratio may be infinite. The infimum is finite because a truthful minimum-total-cost allocation has ratio at most \(m\), so \(1\le R(m)\le m\). A single family must meet its ratio simultaneously for every \(n\) and \(t\); it cannot be chosen after the true instance is known. Different job counts and machine counts may have different rules, and no uniform finite program, computability, representation or time bound is required. The selected problem is an incentive-theoretic extremum over mathematical rules on real reports. A bit encoding or efficient sampling requirement would change that class.

Attainment and asymptotics. The infimum need not be attained. To establish \(R(m)\le u\), it is enough to have admissible families with ratios at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The constants in the requested asymptotic comparison must be independent of \(m\), \(n\), and all processing times. The finite distribution on assignments at each individual report must not be confused with a report-independent finite or countable distribution over entire deterministic truthful mechanisms; the latter is an additional restriction.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.
why: Quantifies how much load-balancing efficiency must be lost solely to multidimensional private costs when randomization and unrestricted payments are available. Matching asymptotic bounds would show whether expected-utility incentives can overcome the linear loss now known for deterministic truthful scheduling.

progress.text: Mu’alem–Schapira prove the lower bound \(2-1/m\), including truthfulness in expectation in §3.4, Theorem 4.
Lu–Yu establish the \((m+5)/2\) truthful-in-expectation upper bound; their linear lower bound has an additional task-independence hypothesis.
Kuryatnikova–Vera nearly determine the optimum for a restricted two-machine, two-job mechanism class.
The proof of the deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture identifies its optimal ratio as \(m\).
A new preprint claims linear lower bounds for countably supported universally truthful mixtures; the broader truthfulness-in-expectation target remains separate.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected unrestricted TIE bounds remain \(2-1/m\le R(m)\le\min\{m,(m+5)/2\}\), leaving its asymptotic order open. The September universal-truthfulness claim has narrower scope; its full proof was not independently certified. The deterministic JACM theorem and restricted two-machine results do not determine this target. The later-work search was bounded.

context_blocks.text: A machine can report a different processing-time vector to reduce the work it receives. Payments give the scheduler a way to counteract that incentive. Because a machine can be fast on one job and slow on another, its type is multidimensional; a single reported speed describes a substantially different model. The goal here measures the schedule at honest reports, while honesty must be optimal even when other machines report arbitrary vectors.

Total processing cost and makespan impose different objectives. A truthful minimum-total-cost allocation assigns each job to a cheapest machine, with appropriate payments. Its makespan is at most its total cost, which is at most the total cost of an optimal makespan assignment and hence at most \(m\operatorname{OPT}(t)\). This explains a universal factor \(m\). With complete information and unlimited computation, an optimal makespan assignment exists; the issue in this card is the additional incentive constraint.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that no deterministic truthful mechanism improves the worst-case factor \(m\). The result was posted in 2023 and published online in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It settles the deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture without a computational hardness assumption. It does not give the same lower bound for truthfulness in expectation.

Universal truthfulness means that the mechanism samples a deterministic truthful rule from a report-independent distribution. Truthfulness in expectation asks only that honest reporting maximize expected utility and permits a larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira prove the lower bound \(2-1/m\) for this larger class. Their theorem allows arbitrary finite processing times, including zero, and is independent of computational limitations.

Lu and Yu give the general truthful-in-expectation guarantee \((m+5)/2\). Together with the deterministic upper bound and the unrestricted randomized lower bound, the inspected literature gives
\[2-\frac1m\le R(m)\le\min\left\{m,\frac{m+5}{2}\right\}.\]
Thus the general gap remains between a constant and a linear function. The same WINE paper reports a linear lower bound under its task-independence restriction; that restricted conclusion cannot be transferred to the whole class defining \(R\).

Correlations matter even when every individual assignment probability is fixed. Take \(m\) unit jobs on \(m\) machines, with every processing time equal to one. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly chosen machine gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\) and makespan \(m\). Assigning the jobs by a uniformly chosen bijection also gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\), but makespan one. Both have expected load one on every machine. Expected utilities depend only on the marginal probabilities and expected payments, whereas expected makespan also depends on the joint assignment distribution.

The 11 September 2026 preprint of Anastasiadis and coauthors claims a lower bound \((3/2-\sqrt2)(m-1)\) for universally truthful mechanisms given by countably supported distributions over deterministic rules, and a universal upper bound \(m/2+o(m)\). The authors discuss extension to uncountable support as an expectation, not a proved theorem. These claims concern a stricter incentive model than this card. In particular, finitely many possible assignments at any fixed report do not imply a countably supported mixture of truthful rules over all reports. The new proof has not been independently certified here.

Small-instance bounds concern different extrema. Kuryatnikova and Vera place the optimal ratio for two machines and two jobs within their randomized monotone, task-independent, scale-free class between \(1.5059953\) and \(1.5059964\). Their scale-free restriction means that multiplying all processing times by one positive constant leaves an allocation rule unchanged. Their mechanisms permit correlated random choices; task independence of a fixed rule is not the same as statistical independence of job assignments. Neither that interval nor the selected restricted mechanism class determines the full \(R(m)\).

A bounded answer would show that randomization keeps the incentive cost of private processing times under control as the system grows. An unbounded answer would show a persistent efficiency loss even with risk-neutral agents and unrestricted transfers. Matching bounds would quantify that loss. Extra assumptions about independent types, Bayesian incentives, fractional execution or computational efficiency describe other questions and cannot be used silently in this one.

The review makes the probability kernel and infimum semantics explicit without specializing to universal truthfulness.
